study_identification_part.si4_title: Individualized cortical thickness asymmetry in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Schizophrenia

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To assess individual-level deviations from normative cortical thickness asymmetry patterns in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) and schizophrenia (SZ) using normative modeling, investigating whether abnormal asymmetry at the individual level is disproportionately represented among these clinical populations.

rci8_quality_checking.detail: Multi-stage quality control: (1) Initial dataset-specific QC - only highest quality ABIDE images included (Bedford et al., 2023); BGS and COBRE images already quality-controlled (Chopra et al., 2023); Utrecht images pre-screened (Janssen et al., 2021). (2) CAT toolbox weighted overall image quality rating (IQR): 682 images excluded with IQR >2.8. (3) FreeSurfer Euler number as proxy for surface quality: 5 images excluded with maximum absolute within-dataset centered Euler number >10. Total exclusions documented in Supplemental Figure 2 flow diagram.
rci8_quality_checking.supporting_text: We initially included only images from ABIDE that we denoted as the highest quality (Bedford et al., 2023). The BGS and COBRE datasets have undergone extensive quality control procedures (Chopra et al., 2023); we initially included the same images from these two samples as (Chopra et al., 2023). For the Utrecht dataset images also underwent extensive quality control and we initially included the same images as (Janssen et al., 2021). (Lines 80-82); we applied the Computational Anatomy Toolbox to generate a weighted overall image quality rating (IQR) for every image (Gaser et al., 2024). This metric combines ratings of basic image properties, including the level of noise and geometric distortions, into a single score that quantifies the overall image quality of a participant's T1-weighted scan (for more information, see Gaser et al. 2024). On this metric, lower scores denote higher image quality. As per previous work, we excluded 682 images with an IQR >2.8 (Wolfers et al., 2018). (Lines 81-83); The Freesurfer Euler number was extracted as a proxy for freesurfer surface quality (Rosen et al., 2018). Finally, as per previous work, images were removed if the maximum, absolute, within-dataset centered Euler number was larger than 10 (Rutherford et al., 2023). This was the case for five images. rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Scanner included as covariate in Bayesian Linear Regression model alongside age, sex, and Euler number. Within-site-split strategy employed where both training and test sets comprised individuals from the same scanners. Post-hoc validation of site effect control: linear support vector classifiers applied to z-scores from training and test HC subsets to classify scan sites. Mean balanced accuracy near chance level (50%) confirmed minimal residual site effects (Supplemental Tables 2-4 show balanced accuracies ranging from 0.43-0.58 for training sets and 0.48-0.66 for test sets across 20 sites, mostly near 0.5).

nm8_nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study employed ten-fold cross-validation on the training cohort to evaluate model generalization. In each fold, 90% of training data was used to train BLR models and 10% reserved for assessing generalization. This process was repeated ten times to generate predictions for all individuals within the training cohort. Root-mean squared error (RMSE) between predicted and true AI values was calculated. While this is non-independent data within the same domain (training dataset), it provides validation of model fit. Results shown in Supplemental Figures 3, 5, and 10 demonstrate RMSE values, which the supplementary text notes are considerably lower than comparable studies (Floris et al. 2021).
nm8_nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To evaluate the generalization of our model, we employed a ten-fold cross-validation approach on the training cohort. Specifically, we divided the training cohort into ten separate folds. In each fold, we trained BLR models using 90% of the participants as training data, while including age, sex, Euler number, and scanner as covariates, reserving the remaining 10% for assessing generalization performance. This process was repeated ten times so that predictions of AI values were generated for all individuals within the training cohort group. This methodology follows standard practices in machine learning and yields nearly unbiased estimates of the model's true generalization capabilities. Z-scores were calculated and we assessed model fit by calculating the root-mean squared error between predicted and true AI values for our main approach and the three alternative approaches (A1, A2 and A3), see Supplemental Figures 3, 5 and 10. (Lines 139-142); Supplemental text states: Regional RMSE values from the current study appear in general considerably lower compared to the voxel-wise RMSE values from Floris et al. caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores calculated as deviation from normative model predictions, normalized by both aleatoric uncertainty (population variance, σr²) and epistemic uncertainty (model uncertainty, σ*r²). Threshold for infra-normal or supra-normal deviation: z ≤ -1.96 or z ≥ 1.96. Regional-level analysis: percentage of individuals with infra/supra-normal deviations per region. Individual-level analysis: number of regions with infra/supra-normal deviations per individual.
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper provides explicit mathematical definition of the z-score calculation including both sources of uncertainty, clearly states the threshold values (±1.96), and describes both regional-level (percentage of individuals per region) and individual-level (number of regions per individual) deviation metrics.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: We calculated z-scores to quantify individual deviations from the normative mean (Lines 49-50); For each region, we assessed the extent to which the AI estimate, for each individual, deviated from the predictions of the normative model. These deviations were quantified as z-scores, for each region (r) and each subject (n), as follows: [formula] where ynr means the true AI and ŷrs is the predicted average AI. The difference in these values is normalized to account for two different sources of variation; i) σr² which is the aleatoric uncertainty and reflects the variation between individuals across the population, and ii) the epistemic uncertainty, σ*r², which accounts for the variance associated to modeling uncertainty introduced by the model structure or parameter selection (associated to the age gaps in which there is low density of individuals). As per prior publications we considered AI z-scores as infra- or supra-normal when they equalled or exceeded -1.96 or 1.96, respectively (Lines 134-138); For each region we calculated, separately for HCtest and each disorder, the percentages of individuals with infra- and supra-normal outlier values (Lines 149-150); For each individual we calculated the number of regions with infra- and supra-normal outlier values (Line 165)

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Regional-level analysis: Permuted chi-square tests (n=10000 permutations) comparing proportions of individuals with infra/supra-normal z-scores between HCtest and each disorder group, with FDR correction (q=0.05) for multiple comparisons; Cohen's ω as effect size measure. Individual-level whole brain analysis: Welch t-tests comparing z-scores for whole brain AI between groups; permuted chi-square tests for proportions of individuals with infra/supra-normal whole brain deviations; Cohen's d and ω as effect size measures. Individual-level regional analysis: Mann-Whitney U tests comparing number of regions with infra/supra-normal z-scores between groups. Multivariate analysis: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding (tSNE) for dimensionality reduction of 160 regional z-scores; k-medoid clustering on tSNE-embedded distance matrix with optimal cluster number determined by average silhouette width; visualization of cluster-diagnosis overlap. Additional analyses: Welch t-tests comparing left- vs right-handers on average z-scores within each group; Pearson correlations between IQ and average z-scores within disorder groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Variation in cortical thickness asymmetry in ASD individuals falls entirely within normative variation; SZ showed minimal differences with only one superior temporal region showing higher proportion of supra-normal deviations (small effect size ω=0.14); multivariate patterns showed no diagnostic differentiation, challenging cortical thickness asymmetry as a biomarker for ASD and SZ.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: For regional analysis, distributions of asymmetry index (AI) z-scores overlapped across HCtest, ASD, and SZ groups for all 160 regions (Supplemental Figure 4). No significant differences were found between HCtest and ASD for any region. For SZ, only one region (superior temporal cortex part 1) showed significantly different proportion of supra-normal deviations compared to HCtest (HCtest=1.14%, SZ=5.92%, χ²=15.45, PFDR<0.05, ω=0.14). Regional infra-normal proportions ranged 0-8.15% (ASD), 0.7-6.7% (SZ), 1.33-4.75% (HCtest); supra-normal proportions ranged 0-8.89% (ASD), 0.7-7.31% (SZ), 0.76-4.56% (HCtest). For whole brain AI, no significant differences in z-scores between HCtest and ASD (Cohen's d=-0.01) or SZ (d=-0.02). Proportions with whole brain infra-normal deviations: HCtest=2.47%, ASD=1.48% (p>0.05, ω=0.05), SZ=3.48% (p>0.05, ω=0.06); supra-normal: HCtest=2.66%, ASD=5.93% (p>0.05, ω=0.15), SZ=3.14% (p>0.05, ω=0.03). For individual-level regional analysis, ASD showed similar distributions to HCtest with no significant differences in average number of infra/supra-normal regions. SZ showed higher average number of both infra-normal (z=-4.21, p<0.01) and supra-normal (z=-4.33, p<0.01) regions compared to HCtest. At least one infra-normal region observed in 93% (ASD), 96% (SZ), 92% (HCtest); at least one supra-normal region in 93% (ASD), 97% (SZ), 96% (HCtest). Multivariate tSNE clustering showed no relationship between regional AI deviation patterns and diagnosis, with nearly identical density plots across groups. Results were consistent across alternative approaches (higher resolution 500-1000 region parcellation, alternative xhemi processing, males-only analysis). No associations found between handedness or IQ and average z-scores within groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Study represents first application of normative modeling framework to regional cortical thickness asymmetry in ASD and SZ. Findings challenge the utility of cortical thickness asymmetry as a biomarker for ASD, as individual abnormal asymmetry appears equally present in ASD, SZ, and healthy controls. Results contrast with smaller-scale studies suggesting asymmetry differences but align with recent large ENIGMA consortium findings showing subtle, non-widespread case-control differences. Authors note that clustering/embedding methods used represent one approach; other multivariate methods considering broader variable sets have successfully identified subgroups in ASD and SZ. The within-site-split validation strategy and post-hoc SVM classifier validation (showing balanced accuracies near chance) provide rigorous evidence that findings are not confounded by residual site effects. Alternative approaches (higher resolution parcellation, alternative asymmetry calculation pipeline, males-only analysis) consistently replicated main findings, demonstrating robustness.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limited training set diversity - while including an Asian dataset, lacks representation from all continents which may affect model generalizability and validity for global populations. Multi-center design necessitated inclusion of datasets lacking deep phenotyping, resulting in incomplete data for handedness, IQ, and symptomatology that limited ability to assess clinical associations. Clinical sample sizes (ASD n=135, SZ n=287) comparable to previous normative modeling studies but larger multicenter samples may enable identification of distinct patient subgroups with significant deviance. Analysis limited to cortical thickness (cortical size property); other properties like cortical volume or novel shape descriptors independent of size may improve explanation of cortical asymmetry variance and clustering performance in multivariate approaches. The preprint status means findings have not undergone formal peer review.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a preprint (medRxiv) posted November 6, 2024, not yet peer-reviewed. The study is notable for being the first to apply normative modeling specifically to cortical thickness asymmetry (rather than absolute cortical thickness) in ASD and SZ. The paper references Supplemental Table 1 for scanner details and demographic characteristics per site (Line 77), but this table is not included in the provided supplementary materials; only Supplemental Tables 2-4 are present (showing SVM balanced accuracy scores for site effect validation). The study includes extensive sensitivity analyses with three alternative approaches: A1 (higher resolution 500-1000 region parcellation using Schaefer atlas), A2 (alternative xhemi cross-hemispheric registration pipeline), and A3 (males-only analysis). The RMSE values for the normative model are reported as considerably lower than the comparable Floris et al. 2021 study (Supplemental Figure 3 and text). The datasets span wide age range (6-95 years for training, 7-65 years for cases) enabling lifespan modeling. Quality control was particularly stringent for ABIDE datasets due to known data quality issues (Bedford et al. 2023). The study employed Romero-Garcia et al. 2014 symmetric parcellation (160 regions of approximately equal size) for primary analysis. Euler number was used both as exclusion criterion (centered absolute >10) and as covariate in models (proxy for FreeSurfer surface reconstruction quality). The within-site-split approach is a strength, ensuring train-test splits occur within scanners rather than across sites.
